title: SDK ambient instrumentation quicklab notes
body:
Purpose

This is a lightweight lab for experimenting with an "ambient" instrumentation layer in Redwood client SDKs. Idea: provide low-friction telemetry and health signals that surface critical developer and product signals without requiring heavy integration work from customers.

Audience
- SDK maintainers (JS, Python)
- DevEx engineers running quickstarts and tutorials
- Solutions/Customer engineers who need minimal telemetry for demos

Primary goals
- Prove a tiny instrumentation contract that is opt-out by default for privacy, opt-in for demos/trials.
- Surface token/latency/cost breakdowns at the SDK level (best-effort).
- Provide an unobtrusive developer UX: single call to enable, transparent docs, no build-time changes.
- Offer quick diagnostics that help users recover from common integration mistakes during the first 10 minutes.

Success metrics for the quicklab (what to measure)
- Time-to-diagnose: median time to identify a misconfigured API key in a demo scenario (target: < 5 mins).
- Opt-in rate for labs (percent of trial accounts that enable ambient telemetry during quicklabs).
- False positive rate for alarms (must be < 2% in synthetic runs).
- Developer sentiment: quick qualitative check from 5 internal devs after running the lab.

Scope for this quick experiment (minimal viable pieces)
1) A tiny runtime shim inside the SDK (JS + Py) that can collect: call start/end timestamps, request size (tokens estimate), response latency, HTTP status, and a hashed operation name.
2) Local-first diagnostics: when an error is detected, emit a human-friendly hint message to the console with a short remediation link.
3) Telemetry sink that can be toggled: console-only / local-file / demo-server endpoint.
4) Example quicklab recipe + reproducible sandbox app that enables instrumentation with a single flag.

Privacy & compliance notes (non-negotiable)
- No user prompt or message content is captured. Strip or hash any user-provided text.
- Make the default OFF for public SDK releases; enable via a clearly labeled demo flag (--enable-ambient-instr = true).
- Provide client-side config to redact anything beyond token counts and latencies.

Minimal telemetry contract (proposal)
- event: request_start | request_end | request_error
- fields: sdk_version, sanitized_model, operation_hash, token_estimate, latency_ms, status_code, region_hint, demo_mode (boolean)
- sample rate: 1% by default, 100% for quicklabs demo server mode

Quick snippet (conceptual)
- JS (pseudo)

  const sdk = RedwoodSDK({apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_KEY, ambientInstr: {enabled:true, mode:'console'}})
  // sdk.generate(...) -> emits console prompts on failure and periodic stats

- Py (pseudo)

  client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.environ['REDWOOD_KEY'], ambient_instr={'enabled': True})
  # wrap calls with short diagnostic hints

UX: developer-facing messages (examples)
- On missing/invalid key: "Redwood SDK: API key not found or rejected (403). Quick tip: set REDWOOD_KEY in your env or run 'rw login'. See: <short link>"
- On high latency: "Redwood SDK: requests to model x are above expected latency (p95 > 2s). Try: enable local caching, reduce sequence length, or switch to a smaller model. See: <short link>"

Quicklab exercises (to include in a 30–45 minute session)
1) Run baseline app with ambient instrumentation disabled. Note console output.
2) Enable ambient mode in console mode. Trigger failures (invalid key, model name typo). Observe hints.
3) Switch sink to demo-server. Inspect received events on the server UI (simple table with filters).
4) Simulate a high token scenario and watch aggregate stats roll up.
5) Flip sample rate to 100% and validate that no content is captured.

Failure modes and risk register (notes to self)
- Overly verbose console hints will annoy users -> keep to 1–2 lines and link to docs.
- Network errors while sending telemetry should never surface to user (silence or exponential backoff).
- Hash collisions for operation_hash could reduce usefulness; use salted HMAC with SDK key fingerprint.

Rollout: staged plan for experiments
- Experiment 0: internal-only quicklab (this doc) + two internal samples (JS + Py).
- Experiment 1: limited public quickstart artifact (flag in examples repo) for select partner demos.
- Experiment 2: decide on default behavior for GA SDKs after privacy review and legal sign-off.

Open questions / TODOs
- Who owns the demo-server UI? quick-ops or devexp? (ASSIGN: Ethan)
- Confirm required legal wording for trial telemetry banner. (ASSIGN: Lina)
- Should we attempt token counting heuristics in the SDK or leave to backend? lightweight heuristics preferred.
- Add an opt-out cookie/setting for web examples?

Implementation checklist (short)
- [ ] design telemetry schema + sample rate config
- [ ] build shim in JS example runner
- [ ] build shim in Python quickrunner
- [ ] demo-server (minimal receiver + UI)
- [ ] small docs page + one-liner for enabling in quicklabs
- [ ] privacy/legal review

Notes and cross-references
- Related ticket: JIRA-ENG-1423 (instrumentation experiments)
- PR seed: github.com/redwood-inference/sdk/pull/1234 (JS shim prototype)
- Design sketch: confluence.redwood/pages/ambient-instr (link to longer writeup)

Quick personal scribbles (informal)
- Keep this tiny. The value is in low friction: developers during a demo should see a helpful nudge not a wall of logs.
- If the demo-server is useful, we can repurpose it for partner integrations and post-mortem export.
- Consider an "assist mode" that runs only in CI/teaching sandboxes and is disabled for production SDKs.

Next steps (for this sprint)
- Pair with Ethan to land the JS shim into examples repo (3 days).
- Create the minimal demo-server and a quick UI (5 days).
- Run internal quicklab with 5 engineers and collect feedback (1 week after landing).
